passage:
Monday. Karthik had his guitar case by the door when Binita sighed down the phone. "Go, enjoy. I'll just sit here alone again." He put the guitar back. Band practice happened without him.
Thursday. He had skipped three practices in two weeks. Sitting in the college library, he made two lists. One: times he had actually let Binita down, like arriving an hour late to her exam-result dinner. He had apologised for that, and meant it. Two: times he felt guilty only because she sulked. The second list was much longer.
The following Monday. "I'm going to practice tonight," he told her. "I'll call you at nine." Binita went quiet, then said, "Fine, whatever you want." His stomach twisted, but he picked up the guitar. At nine he called, as promised. She was cool at first, then asked about the new song.

qa.q: How many practices had Karthik skipped in two weeks?
qa.a: Karthik had skipped three practices in two weeks.

qa.q: What did Karthik feel when Binita said "Fine, whatever you want"?
qa.a: He felt guilty and uneasy, his stomach twisting, because her coolness still pulled at him even though he had done nothing wrong.

qa.q: Why was Karthik's two-list exercise in the library a turning point?
qa.a: It helped him separate a real wrong, the late dinner that deserved an apology, from guilt that came only from sulking, so he could go to practice and still keep his promise to call.

qa.q: How might Binita experience Karthik going to practice and calling at nine?
qa.a: She may feel left out at first, which is why she went quiet, but the promised call showed he still cared, and she warmed up enough to ask about the new song.

grounding: A young man keeps giving up band practice when Binita sighs and sulks, then sorts real wrongs from pressure and goes while keeping in touch.

passage:
Wasim, you check your phone every time your mother calls, even mid-shift. Your Damini Aunty has nursed on this ward for thirty years. Listen to something from when I was twenty.
My Ammi raised four of us alone, and she never let me forget it. If I wanted to join the college trip, she would say, "Go. Who am I? Only the one who sold her bangles for your fees." Then she would not eat dinner. So I stayed. I missed the trip, the drama club, my best friend's wedding.
On the wedding day I was home, and Ammi was watching television, perfectly cheerful. I realised my staying had not made her happy. It had only stopped the sighing.
The next year I joined the drama club. I called her every evening at eight and let her sulk without fixing it. She sulked for a month. Then she came to my first play, in her best dupatta.

qa.q: What did Damini miss while she kept staying home?
qa.a: She missed the college trip, the drama club and her best friend's wedding.

qa.q: What did young Damini feel when she saw Ammi cheerful on the wedding day?
qa.a: She felt a jolt of clarity mixed with sadness, realising her staying had not made Ammi happy but had only stopped the sighing.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story changed things for young Damini?
qa.a: Joining the drama club while calling Ammi every evening at eight let her keep her own life and her care, without rushing to fix the sulking.

qa.q: How might Ammi have felt when she came to the first play?
qa.a: Ammi likely felt proud and a little relieved, and the best dupatta suggests the sulking had given way to respect for Damini's choice.

grounding: A senior nurse tells Wasim how, at twenty, she kept giving in to her mother's sighs and reminders of sacrifice until she chose her own plans while still calling home.
